senses.ex: Es más caro que el otro.
senses.en: It's more expensive than the other one.

note: `qué` with an accent is the question word. Unstressed `que` is the workhorse that glues clauses together, and in fast speech it is barely pronounced at all.

senses.g: the ... part (lo + adjective makes an abstract noun)
senses.en: The hard part is the price.
I didn't understand what he said.

note: `lo` is never 'the' in front of a masculine noun -- that is `el`. With an adjective it means 'the ... thing', which has no tidy English equivalent.

senses.en: He doesn't live here any more.

note: Mostly carried by tone. With `no` it always means 'not any more' -- `ya no` is worth hearing as a single word.

senses.g: impersonal / passive: one does, it is done
it happened to me (no one is blamed)
reflexive, or a change of state
stands in for le / les before lo / la
senses.en: I gave it to the owner.

note: Four unrelated jobs, one syllable. Chapter 10 has the full picture.

senses.en: Since he didn't turn up, we left.

note: `cómo` with an accent asks 'how'. Unstressed `como` means 'like' or 'roughly'.

senses.en: I don't like it at all.

senses.g: so, that (before an adjective or adverb)

note: `tan` goes before adjectives and adverbs; `tanto` goes with verbs and nouns.

senses.g: because of, for the sake of (a cause)
senses.en: I bought it for the land.
To sign, I need the title.

note: Rule of thumb that survives most cases: `por` looks backwards at a cause, `para` looks forwards at a goal.

senses.g: even if (with the subjunctive, a hypothetical)
senses.en: Even if it's expensive, I want it.

note: The verb mood is the whole difference: indicative concedes something true, subjunctive supposes something that may not be.

senses.ex: No es el precio, sino los gastos.
senses.en: It isn't the price, it's the fees.

note: Only after a negative, and it replaces rather than adds. `pero` adds a qualification; `sino` corrects the thing just denied.

senses.en: While we signed, she waited outside.

senses.ex: Mientras no firmes, no hay trato.
senses.en: As long as you don't sign, there's no deal.

senses.ex: Según el plano, son mil metros.
senses.en: According to the plan, it's a thousand metres.
Depending on how it turns out, we'll decide.
As soon as he arrives, I'll call you.
As soon as I sign, I'll let you know.

senses.ex: Ni el precio ni los linderos están claros.
senses.en: Neither the price nor the boundaries are clear.
It's on top of the table.

senses.g: on top of that (piling on a complaint)
senses.ex: Y encima me cobró la notaría.
senses.en: And on top of that he charged me the notary fee.
That's why I want to see it first.

senses.ex: Ya que estamos aquí, veamos el lindero.
senses.en: Since we're here, let's look at the boundary.

senses.ex: De todas formas hay que firmar.
senses.en: Either way, we have to sign.
Each lot has its own deed.

note: `cualquier` goes before a noun; `cualquiera` stands on its own.

senses.en: Is there any problem with the title?

note: Spanish doubles the negative and both halves are compulsory: `no` on the verb and `ningún` on the noun. Dropping the `no` sounds wrong, not emphatic.
Never `un otro`. 'Another' is just `otro`.

senses.ex: Me lo dijo el propio dueño.

senses.en: The rest of the documents arrive tomorrow.
It's quite far from the town.

senses.g: kind of, a bit (before an adjective)
senses.en: The road is kind of a mess.

senses.ex: El lindero va hacia el río.
senses.en: The boundary runs towards the river.
You can see it from the road.

senses.ex: El terreno llega hasta el lindero.
senses.en: The land goes as far as the boundary.

note: In Mexico and Central America `hasta` often carries a hidden 'not': `Llega hasta las tres` usually means he doesn't get there until three.
Latin America prefers `acá` and `allá` over `aquí` and `allí`; they are vaguer about the exact spot, which is usually the point.

senses.en: The well is back over there.
Well, I don't know what to tell you.

senses.ex: Si no te gusta, pues no lo compres.
senses.en: If you don't like it, then don't buy it.

note: Enormously common and nearly meaningless. Often reduced to `pos` or a single hissed syllable. Do not go looking for content in it.

senses.g: I mean, that is to say

note: The commonest repair phrase in spoken Spanish. When you hear it, a clarification is coming -- listen to what follows, not to what you just missed.

senses.ex: Es que no tengo el plano todavía.
senses.en: The thing is, I don't have the survey plan yet.

note: Introduces an explanation, and very often a refusal in polite clothing.
`claro que sí` and `claro que no` are emphatic. A bare `claro` is just 'right' -- agreement, not necessarily enthusiasm.

senses.en: Right, so we'll sign on Monday.

note: At the start of a turn it means 'right then', not 'good'. Answering the phone in Mexico, it means 'hello'.
In much of South America a clause-initial `igual` softens to 'anyway' or even 'maybe'. It is not about equality.
Dangerously elastic. In Mexico and Central America it stretches from 'this second' to 'at some point'. Never hear it as a commitment to a time.

senses.en: Get this -- he never called me.

note: `fíjate que` nearly always introduces bad news or a complication.

senses.ex: De repente se levantó y se fue.
senses.en: He suddenly got up and left.

note: In Peru this usually means 'maybe'. Taking it as 'suddenly' turns a vague plan into an event that never happened.

senses.g: keeping an eye on (estar pendiente de)
senses.en: I'm keeping an eye on the payment.
